<GithubRepo url="https://github.com/arkitektio/esp32-embassy-demo" title="esp32-embassy-demo" />

Not every device in a lab can run Python. A stage controller, a shutter, a temperature probe or a
pump often sits behind a microcontroller. Such a board can be an Arkitekt
[agent](/docs/about/terminology#agent) of its own: it registers actions that anyone in your
organization can call from Orkestrator, a script or a workflow, and it publishes live state, with
no computer in between.

**We use Rust for this as well.** There is no separate embedded SDK and no C++ firmware library.
A microcontroller runs the same crates as a [desktop Rust app](/docs/build/rust/first-app): the
same `App`, the same `#[action]`, the same `#[derive(State)]`. What changes is the platform
underneath. On a board there is no operating system, so the crates are built without the standard
library and run on [embassy](https://embassy.dev), an async runtime for bare metal.

<Callout type="warn" title="Experimental">

The embedded stack is young and changes quickly. The demo below is the reference, and it is a
demo: it shows that the whole path works on a board, and it is the starting point for your own
firmware. [What is not there yet](/docs/build/embedded/reference#what-is-not-there-yet) lists the
gaps. Do not use it for safety-relevant hardware.

</Callout>

<Prerequisites>

- An **ESP32-S3** board (the demo targets the ESP32-S3-DevKitC-1) or a classic **ESP32**, with at
  least 4 MB of flash
- The Espressif Rust toolchain, installed with [`espup`](https://github.com/esp-rs/espup)
- A running hub, and Orkestrator on a computer with Bluetooth, to provision the device
- A Wi-Fi network (WPA2-Personal, or WPA2-Enterprise such as eduroam) from which the device can
  reach your Arkitekt server

</Prerequisites>

<Learn>

- Why embedded devices use the Rust client, and what differs from a desktop app
- What the `esp32-embassy-demo` firmware does from power-on to its first task
- How its actions and states are declared
- Build, flash and provision a board

</Learn>

## The demo

[`esp32-embassy-demo`](https://github.com/arkitektio/esp32-embassy-demo) is a complete firmware
that turns an ESP32 into an agent. Everything on the board is Rust: there is no ESP-IDF and no
C SDK underneath.

It offers a handful of actions and two states, chosen to exercise every part of the path:

| | What it does |
|---|---|
| `echo` | Returns the text it was given. Proves a task makes the round trip. |
| `free_heap` | Returns the free heap in KiB |
| `set_led` | Switches the board's RGB LED on or off (ESP32-S3) |
| `set_led_color` | Lights the LED in a colour, from red, green and blue values (ESP32-S3) |
| `Sensors` state | The chip temperature, the Wi-Fi signal, the free heap and how often the BOOT button was pressed |
| `Led` state | Whether the LED is on, and its colour |

Once it is running you can call `set_led_color` from Orkestrator and watch the `Led` state follow,
or press the BOOT button on the board and see `presses` count up in the UI. That is the whole
model from [shared concepts](/docs/build/shared-concepts) on a chip the size of a stamp.

## From power-on to the first task

1. **Identity.** The device derives its id from its MAC address, so it keeps the same identity
   across reflashes.
2. **Provisioning over Bluetooth.** From boot it advertises itself as `ARKITEKT-xxxx`. In
   Orkestrator, under **Lok → Provision a device**, you pick it. Orkestrator issues a key for it
   and sends the Wi-Fi credentials, the address of your deployment and the key in one document.
   The device stores it in flash.
3. **Wi-Fi.** It joins the network, including enterprise networks such as eduroam.
4. **Clock.** It sets its clock over SNTP. A certificate cannot be checked without knowing the
   date.
5. **Login.** It logs in with the key it was given. There is no browser on a microcontroller, so
   the key from provisioning stands in for the approval a person gives a desktop app.
6. **Agent.** It opens the [agent socket](/docs/build/agent-protocol), registers its actions and
   states, and waits for tasks.
7. **Bluetooth off.** Five seconds after registering, Bluetooth is switched off and its memory is
   given back to the app.

Holding the BOOT button for 5 seconds while the device starts erases its configuration and login,
and it returns to step 2.

## How the actions are written

This is the part that should look familiar. The demo's actions are ordinary `#[action]` functions,
identical in form to the ones in [Your first Rust app](/docs/build/rust/first-app):

```rust
/// Free heap
///
/// How much heap the device has left, in KiB.
///
/// # Returns
/// Free heap in KiB
#[action]
async fn free_heap() -> i64 {
    (esp_alloc::HEAP.free() / 1024) as i64
}
```

State is a struct deriving `State`, and an action that changes hardware updates it:

```rust
/// The board's LED, as the actions left it.
#[derive(Clone, Debug, Serialize, Deserialize, State)]
#[state(name = "Led")]
struct LedState {
    /// Whether the LED is on
    on: bool,
    /// The colour it shows when on, as #rrggbb
    color: String,
}

/// LED
///
/// Switches the board's LED on or off.
///
/// # Arguments
/// * `on` - Whether the LED should be on
///
/// # Returns
/// Whether the LED is on now
#[action]
async fn set_led(on: bool, state: StateMut<LedState>) -> anyhow::Result<bool> {
    led::set(on);                      // drive the pin
    state.set(LedState::now())?;       // publish what it is now
    Ok(state.read(|led| led.on))
}
```

The `Sensors` state is kept current by a **background hook**, which reads the chip once a second.
It publishes a value only when it moved by a meaningful step (half a degree, 3 dB), so sensor
noise does not turn into a stream of patches.

The app is declared exactly as on a desktop:

```rust
let app = App::new("live.arkitekt.esp32-embassy", "1")
    .action(echo)
    .action(free_heap)
    .state(sensors::read())
    .background(sensors::report)
    .state(LedState::now())
    .action(set_led)
    .action(set_led_color);
```

What differs is how it is run. A desktop app calls `run(app)`. A board has no operating system to
provide a network, a clock or randomness, so the firmware hands those over as a `Board` and
connects on it:

```rust
let board = Board { host: &HOST, tcp, dns, verify: verify() };
let runtime = Runtime::connect(board, app, options).await?;
runtime.serve().await?;
```

## Build and flash

Install the toolchain once, then build, flash and open the serial monitor in one step:

```sh
espup install
. ~/export-esp.sh

cargo esp32s3     # an ESP32-S3
cargo esp32       # a classic ESP32
```

The image is about 2.4 MB. Then provision the device from Orkestrator under
**Lok → Provision a device**. It appears under **Apps** with its actions and its two states.

<Callout type="info" title="Until the crates are published">

The demo currently depends on sibling checkouts: the provisioning crate from
[`arkitekt-esp32-rs`](https://github.com/arkitektio/arkitekt-esp32-rs), and unreleased versions of
the arkirust crates. Its
[README](https://github.com/arkitektio/esp32-embassy-demo#build-and-flash) says which repositories
to place side by side.

</Callout>

Next: the [Embedded reference](/docs/build/embedded/reference) covers the crates, TLS, memory and
what is not there yet.

<Quiz>
  <Question q="Which client does an embedded device use?">
    The Rust client. A microcontroller runs the same crates as a desktop Rust app, with the same `App`, `#[action]` and `#[derive(State)]`, built without the standard library on embassy.
  </Question>
  <Question q="How does a device with no screen or browser get authorized?">
    It is provisioned over Bluetooth from Orkestrator, which issues a key and sends it together with the Wi-Fi credentials and the deployment's address. The device logs in with that key.
  </Question>
  <Question q="What differs between a desktop Rust app and the firmware?">
    Not the actions or the states, but how the app is run: the firmware passes the network, clock and randomness of the board in as a `Board` and calls `Runtime::connect` on it, where a desktop app calls `run(app)`.
  </Question>
</Quiz>
